strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: reward design for RL alignment of text-to-image models, where interpretability, prompt adaptivity, and controllability are genuinely valuable goals.

The proposed rubric formulation is simple and intuitive: generate prompt-specific criteria, score each criterion independently, and aggregate them into a reward. This gives a clearer diagnostic signal than a single opaque scalar reward.
The experiments cover two autoregressive backbones and two standard benchmarks, with comparisons against several single-reward and composite-reward alternatives under a shared GRPO training setup.
The ablations on rollout sampling, advantage normalization, grader model choice, and oversampling budget are useful and help isolate some design choices beyond the headline method.
The paper includes a candid failure analysis showing that the GPT-o4-mini grader can misjudge counting cases, especially when image quality is poor.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is relatively incremental. Rubric generation plus VLM-based judging is a natural extension of LLM-as-judge/rubric reward ideas, and the aggregation is just a binary mean over ten criteria. The dynamic rollout sampling component is also simple and not deeply analyzed theoretically.

The method depends heavily on GPT-o4-mini for rubric generation, rubric selection, and image grading. This creates major reproducibility concerns due to a proprietary, changing API, unclear prompts, unclear decoding settings, and potentially high training-time cost. The paper does not provide enough detail to reproduce the reward pipeline faithfully.
The claimed generality to diffusion models is not experimentally supported. All main experiments are on AR text-to-image models, so the architecture-agnostic claim remains speculative.

The evaluation relies almost entirely on automatic benchmarks. Since the method optimizes against a powerful VLM judge, human preference studies or independent blind evaluation would be important to rule out benchmark-specific or judge-specific reward effects.

There are signs of fragility in the results: on Qwen2.5-0.5B, RubricRL underperforms the SFT model on counting in GenEval and on the DPG-Bench Other category, and several gains over baselines are modest. No variance over seeds, confidence intervals, or significance analysis is reported.

The training setup is underspecified in several important places, including the exact rubric prompts, number of rubric-generation queries, filtering rules for malformed rubrics, value of K in hybrid sampling, reward API settings, cost/latency, and whether rubrics are cached.

The baseline comparison may not be fully convincing. The authors reimplement several reward methods but do not provide enough evidence that these reimplementations are tuned comparably to the proposed method. Some table formatting issues also make several numbers hard to parse.

Selecting top-reward rollouts before computing GRPO updates changes the training distribution and may introduce optimization bias; the paper treats this empirically but does not discuss possible reward overfitting or exploitation of grader weaknesses.

The presentation has numerous grammar, formatting, and citation issues, including malformed tables, inconsistent model names such as GPT-o4-mini/o4-mini, and some questionable references, which reduces clarity and confidence in the experimental reporting.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely problem: reward design for RL alignment of text-to-image generators, where interpretability and prompt-specific evaluation are genuinely important.
The proposed rubric-based formulation is simple and intuitive. Decomposing rewards into per-criterion binary judgments could be useful for debugging and user control if implemented robustly.

Experiments cover two AR backbones, Phi3-3.8B and Qwen2.5-0.5B, and two common benchmarks, GenEval and DPG-Bench. The reported overall gains over SFT and several reward baselines suggest the idea may have practical value.

The paper includes some relevant ablations, including grader model strength, rollout sampling strategy, advantage normalization scope, and Best-of-N comparison. It also acknowledges a real failure mode of the VLM grader on counting.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The core method is essentially LLM-generated checklists plus VLM-as-judge rewards, averaged and plugged into GRPO. The paper does not convincingly distinguish this from existing multimodal LLM reward models or rubric-as-reward work beyond applying it to T2I.

Several major claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly claims architecture-agnostic applicability to diffusion and AR models, but all experiments are on AR models only. No diffusion experiment or analysis is provided, so the generality claim is unsupported.

The method description is internally inconsistent. The abstract and introduction claim a prompt-adaptive weighting mechanism, but the actual reward in Eq. 3 is an unweighted mean of ten binary rubric scores. This weakens the claimed contribution around adaptive weighting and composability.

The evidence is not strong enough for the claims. There is no human preference evaluation, no statistical significance or variance across runs, and no study of reward hacking or correlation between rubric scores and human judgments. For a reward-design paper, validating the reward itself is essential.

The dependence on proprietary GPT-o4-mini/o4-style judging creates serious reproducibility and deployment concerns. API prompts, decoding parameters, cost, latency, exact rubric filtering rules, and grader calibration are underspecified. The strongest results depend on the strongest closed grader, as shown by the Qwen grader ablation.

Important ablations are missing. The paper does not compare against a direct VLM scalar judge without generated rubrics, fixed hand-written rubrics, non-binary scoring, rubric-only evaluation without RL, or using the same VLM judge in existing reward formulations. Thus it is unclear whether the gains come from rubrics, from o4-mini quality, or from the rollout-selection heuristic.

The rollout-level dynamic sampling method is weakly justified and potentially biased: selecting top-reward samples from oversampled rollouts changes the training distribution and may amplify grader errors. The paper reports benchmark scores but provides little theoretical or empirical analysis of stability, bias, or reward overoptimization.

Some reported results undercut the broad conclusions. For Qwen2.5-0.5B, RubricRL hurts GenEval counting relative to SFT and Best-of-N, and DPG-Bench “Other” is worse than SFT. The paper attributes this to grader counting failures, but that is a significant limitation for a rubric-based visual reward method.

Baseline fairness is hard to assess. The authors say they reimplement several baselines under the same GRPO framework, but do not provide enough implementation details, hyperparameters, reward scaling choices, or tuning budgets. This is especially important because small changes in RL reward normalization and sampling can materially affect results.

Presentation quality is poor for an ECCV submission. There are many grammar issues, formatting problems, crowded or malformed tables, and even apparent citation/reference problems. For example, the Chameleon citation appears to reference an unrelated 1999 clustering paper. These issues do not alone determine rejection, but they reduce confidence in care and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: reward design for RL alignment of text-to-image generators. The proposed rubric-based formulation is simple, intuitive, and well motivated relative to fixed multi-reward mixtures and opaque scalar preference models.

RubricRL provides a clear practical advantage: the reward decomposes into human-readable criteria, which improves interpretability, debugging, and potential user control. This is a meaningful contribution even though the core mechanism is conceptually straightforward.

The empirical results are consistently positive across two AR backbones, Phi3-3.8B and Qwen2.5-0.5B, and two standard benchmarks, GenEval and DPG-Bench. The gains over SFT and several reward baselines are particularly convincing for the stronger Phi3 backbone.

The ablations are useful and relevant. The paper studies dynamic rollout sampling, local vs global advantage normalization, Best-of-N sampling, grader strength, and rollout budget, which helps separate the effect of the rubric reward from the proposed training details.

The manuscript is generally clear and easy to follow, with qualitative examples and failure cases that make the behavior of the method interpretable. The acknowledgement of grader counting errors is valuable and strengthens the credibility of the analysis.
weaknesses: There is an important inconsistency between the claimed method and the implemented method. The abstract and introduction describe a prompt-adaptive weighting mechanism, but the method section appears to use a simple unweighted mean over 10 binary rubric scores. This weakens the technical precision of the claimed contribution.

The method relies heavily on GPT-o4-mini for both rubric generation and grading. This raises reproducibility, cost, latency, and availability concerns, and the paper does not sufficiently quantify these practical constraints. The supplementary grader ablation helps, but the main reported performance still depends on a closed proprietary model.

The architecture-agnostic claim is broader than the evidence. Experiments are only conducted on autoregressive T2I models; no diffusion-model experiment is provided despite repeated claims that the approach applies equally to diffusion architectures.

Novelty is moderate rather than high. Using LLM/VLM-generated rubrics as rewards is a natural extension of recent rubric-based RL ideas and VLM-as-judge pipelines. The paper’s value is mostly in adapting and validating the idea for T2I RL, not in a fundamentally new algorithmic insight.

The evaluation would be stronger with human preference studies or blind human assessment, since the main claim concerns human-aligned visual quality and interpretability. Benchmark scores and qualitative examples are useful, but they do not fully establish that the rubric rewards better match human preferences.

Several experimental details remain underspecified for reproducibility, including the exact prompts used for rubric generation/grading, filtering rules for malformed rubrics, API settings, stochasticity controls, and the compute/API cost of generating many rollouts and rubric scores.

The failure analysis shows that weak base models can be harmed on counting-related categories due to grader mistakes. This is an important limitation: RubricRL’s success appears coupled to both generator quality and grader reliability, and the method may be vulnerable to reward noise or reward hacking in longer training runs.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practically useful formulation: prompt-specific, human-readable rubrics scored independently by a multimodal judge and aggregated into an RL reward for text-to-image generation. The decomposition gives a more inspectable reward signal than a single scalar preference model and is easy to integrate with existing GRPO/DiffusionNFT pipelines.

The empirical evaluation is broader than many RL-for-T2I papers: results are reported on GenEval and DPG-Bench across two autoregressive backbones and two diffusion/flow backbones, with consistent gains over SFT and several reward baselines. The gains on GenEval are especially strong, e.g. Phi3 improves from 0.7624 SFT and 0.8080 X-Omni to 0.8468, and Qwen-Image improves from 0.8406 to 0.9091.

The paper includes useful ablations on binary vs continuous scoring, number of rubrics, grader model size, rollout selection, advantage normalization, and Best-of-N sampling. These help isolate some design choices and show that the method depends meaningfully on rubric count and grader quality.

The authors acknowledge and analyze important failure modes of the GPT-o4-mini grader, especially counting errors under ambiguous or low-quality generations. They also provide a cost/accessibility discussion and a human study for rubric consistency and judge agreement, which strengthens the practical assessment.

The method is simple and modular. Even if not algorithmically complex, the contribution type is best assessed as an Algorithms/General systems-style reward design for T2I alignment, and the paper provides enough evidence that this design can improve multiple model families.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate. The core idea is essentially LLM/VLM-as-judge with generated rubrics and mean binary scoring, which is a natural extension of rubric-based rewards already explored in language domains. The paper claims first use for T2I RL, but the conceptual novelty beyond prompt-adaptive checklists plus an existing multimodal judge is limited.

The strongest results rely on a proprietary and expensive GPT-o4-mini grader for both rubric generation and scoring. Open-source grader ablations lag substantially, so the method's reproducibility, accessibility, and deployability are weaker than the headline suggests. API/version stochasticity and exact inference settings are not specified enough to make the reward fully reproducible.

There is possible benchmark coupling. The supplementary rubric selection prompt explicitly prioritizes GenEval indicators and DPG-Bench indicators, while the main quantitative claims are evaluated on GenEval and DPG-Bench. This makes the generalization claims less convincing and raises concern that the reward design is partially tuned to the evaluation benchmarks rather than measuring broad prompt-following ability.

The human studies are encouraging but under-specified. The paper gives sample sizes and aggregate agreement/preference rates, but lacks important details such as annotator recruitment/qualification, number of ratings per item, inter-annotator agreement, confidence intervals, significance tests, and whether annotators were independent of the authors. The preference plots are also hard to interpret quantitatively from the paper text.

The reward is vulnerable to judge bias and reward hacking. Since the same powerful VLM supplies binary labels during training, the learned policy may optimize quirks of that judge rather than human visual judgment. The paper shows some agreement with humans, but the study is small relative to the training/evaluation space and does not test adversarial or out-of-distribution prompts.

Several experimental confounds remain. RubricRL includes dynamic rollout sampling and local normalization choices, while comparisons are framed mainly as reward-function comparisons. Although there are ablations, it is not always clear how much of the improvement comes from the rubric reward itself versus rollout selection, benchmark-specific rubric selection, or implementation details.

The paper reports no variance over random seeds and limited statistical uncertainty for benchmark improvements. Some DPG gains are modest, and certain categories degrade, such as Qwen2.5 DPG Global/Other and Qwen2.5 GenEval Counting relative to some baselines/SFT. These weaknesses are discussed only partially.

strengths: No explicit contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. The paper tackles an important and timely problem: reward design for RL post-training of text-to-image generators, where interpretability, controllability, and prompt-specific feedback are genuinely relevant concerns.

The rubric decomposition is easy to understand and operationally appealing. Per-criterion binary scores could be useful for diagnostics compared with a single opaque scalar reward, and the paper includes concrete prompt templates in the supplement.

The experimental scope is reasonably broad on the surface: AR and diffusion backbones, GenEval and DPG-Bench, several reward baselines, ablations on rollout sampling, binary versus continuous scoring, number of rubrics, grader model size, and some human evaluation.

The reported headline numbers show consistent overall improvements on several settings, especially GenEval for Phi3 and diffusion backbones, suggesting that rubric-based VLM feedback can be a useful training signal.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is quite thin. The method largely consists of prompting GPT-o4-mini to generate rubrics and then prompting it again for binary pass/fail judgments, followed by standard GRPO/DiffusionNFT. This is a straightforward extension of LLM/VLM-as-judge and rubric-as-reward ideas, and the paper does not provide much algorithmic novelty beyond prompt engineering and top-K rollout selection.

There is a major inconsistency between the claimed method and the actual formulation: the abstract and introduction claim a prompt-adaptive weighting mechanism, but the method computes the final reward as an unweighted mean over 10 binary criteria. This weakens confidence in the presentation and in the claimed contribution.

The evidence is not sufficiently convincing for the breadth of the claims. Some subcategories degrade substantially: for Qwen2.5 on GenEval, counting slightly drops relative to SFT; on DPG-Bench, Qwen2.5 global and other scores drop sharply, and the authors acknowledge counting failures. These are important failures for a method claiming prompt faithfulness and fine-grained control.

The evaluation risks benchmark overfitting. The rubric-selection prompt explicitly prioritizes GenEval and DPG-Bench indicators, and the paper also rewrites prompts for evaluation. This makes the reported gains hard to interpret as general reward quality rather than optimization toward the chosen benchmarks and evaluators.

Reproducibility is weak. The method depends centrally on proprietary GPT-o4-mini/o4-mini API behavior, but model versioning, sampling settings, seeds, retry/parsing behavior, and release details are not specified adequately. The cost is also substantial, about $1.18K per epoch, making independent reproduction difficult.

Baseline fairness is unclear. The baselines are reimplemented under the authors' RL framework, but there is limited detail on tuning, reward scaling, dynamic rollout selection compatibility, and whether each baseline received comparable optimization effort. Some results look suspicious, e.g. LLaVA-Reward-Phi exactly matching SFT for Qwen2.5 in multiple tables.

The human studies are underreported. The paper gives headline agreement/preference percentages but lacks important details such as annotator recruitment, number of judgments per item, inter-annotator agreement, confidence intervals, tie handling, statistical significance, and full numerical results for the plotted preference figures.

The reliability study does not fully validate the training signal. A 94.8% agreement claim over selected rubric-image judgments is encouraging, but the paper simultaneously shows concrete GPT-o4-mini counting failures, and there is no analysis of how often such failures occur during RL or how reward noise affects policy updates.

The dynamic rollout sampling component confounds the contribution. The method selects top-reward rollouts from 16 candidates and trains on 4, which is itself a strong filtering/best-of-N-like mechanism. The paper does not cleanly separate gains from rubric quality versus selection bias and oversampling.

Writing and rigor issues further reduce confidence: duplicated supplement sections, inconsistent prompt-output format descriptions, awkward equations/text extraction artifacts, overbroad claims of generalizability and controllability, and limited discussion of failure modes relative to the strength of the claims. Overall, the work has some empirical promise but is not yet a convincing ECCV-level contribution.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, well-motivated reward-design framework for text-to-image RL: prompt-specific rubrics are generated, independently judged, and aggregated into a reward. This directly addresses interpretability and controllability limitations of fixed composite metrics and opaque scalar reward models.

Empirical support is broad and appropriate for an Algorithms/General contribution. RubricRL is evaluated on both autoregressive and diffusion/flow backbones, across GenEval and DPG-Bench, and usually improves over SFT, single-reward, unified-reward, and composite-reward baselines. The gains on GenEval for diffusion models and on Phi3 are especially convincing.

The ablation suite is useful: binary vs. continuous rewards, number of rubrics, grader model quality, rollout sampling, advantage normalization, Best-of-N comparison, aesthetic evaluation, and human preference/judge-alignment studies all help substantiate the central design choices.

The method has practical appeal because the rubrics expose interpretable failure modes and user-adjustable reward dimensions. The supplementary prompt templates and cost discussion improve transparency and reproducibility relative to many VLM-as-reward papers.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is moderate: the main idea is to use a strong proprietary VLM to generate and grade checklist-style criteria, then plug the resulting scalar reward into existing RL optimizers. The dynamic rollout sampling is sensible but relatively simple, so the contribution rests heavily on empirical validation rather than a deep new optimization method.

Dependence on GPT-o4-mini is a significant reproducibility and accessibility concern. The authors show weaker results with open-source Qwen2.5-VL graders and report nontrivial API cost, but the strongest claims still rely on a closed, changing model whose behavior may be hard to reproduce exactly.

There is some evaluator/reward coupling risk. Rubrics are prioritized partly around GenEval/DPG-style criteria, training images are re-captioned with o4-mini, and o4-mini is also used for reward generation/grading. Although external benchmarks and human studies mitigate this, the setup could still overfit to VLM-judged prompt-following rather than broader human preference.

The method has known failure modes on counting and ambiguous scenes; on the weaker Qwen2.5-0.5B backbone, RubricRL can underperform SFT in some counting/Other categories. This suggests reward noise can become problematic when base generations are poor, and the paper could better characterize when the grader is reliable enough for RL.

Several experimental details are underspecified or could be stronger, including statistical significance across seeds, exact annotator protocol and agreement statistics, top-K choice in hybrid rollout selection, API decoding settings, and release plans for rubrics, prompts, code, and trained checkpoints. Some presentation issues and table formatting glitches also reduce clarity.
